# Phase gates 12, 13 and 15 — stage 2 findings

Run 2026-08-14 at HEAD `108ea25`, tree clean. Three blind lenses per phase, each unable to see
the others; one adjudicator per phase merging and re-grading; two skeptics per surviving MAJOR,
each briefed to REFUTE it. **Refuting takes both skeptics** — a tie upholds, and a skeptic that
died has said nothing rather than said no.

62 agents, 4,792,098 tokens, 2h58m. Stage 1 was measured by the orchestrator beforehand and not
re-derived: gate 1280/1280 five legs GATE PASS, M5 128 files, ctest 92 cases / 27,726 assertions,
acceptance 16 PASS / 5 FAIL in a fresh worktree.

### Confirmed MAJORs (6)

#### 1. G5 equivalence step not discharged: the two "arms" differ only by an env var no code reads

`scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py:1503` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**Claim.** Plan:2884-2888 mandates "run Task 13.1's scripted e2e twice — once with the router in the loop, once with --no-router — and assert the same terminal state, the same item dispositions, and the same commit set", explicitly to make "the identical process runs without the router" true rather than aspirational. What shipped is a python unit test comparing two config dicts / env dicts / argv lists (it never runs the e2e), plus a recorded artifact whose two arms are the same command run twice under CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL — a variable that appears nowhere in the codebase. The named driver conductor/tests/e2e-g5.test.ts does not exist.

**Failure scenario.** docs/build/artifacts/12.1-g5-equivalence.md:65 and :90 record arm A and arm B as `node --test conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts` under CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL=:8088 and :8080 respectively. I confirmed `grep -rn CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL conductor/ scripts/` returns zero hits and `ls conductor/tests/e2e-g5.test.ts` says No such file. The two arms were therefore byte-identical executions with an inert environment variable; the artifact itself measures the router's ledger gaining 0 rows during arm A. A router that broke every pipeline interaction would produce the same "IDENTICAL" verdict. The comparison the plan requires — terminal state, item dispositions, commit set, across a real router process and no router process — has never been made.

**How to prove it.** Run `CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1/v1 bash scripts/test-conductor.sh conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts` (a dead port belonging to neither arm). Expected: TAP tests=5 pass=5, GATE PASS — the variable that supposedly distinguished the arms has no effect. Then `grep -rn 'CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL' conductor/ scripts/` (0 hits, confirmed) and `ls conductor/tests/e2e-g5.test.ts` (absent, confirmed).

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* Every load-bearing claim in the finding reproduced exactly as stated, and the proposed proof produced precisely the predicted outcome.

The decisive run is item 3: the e2e passes 5/5 and the whole gate passes with CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL set to a dead port (127.0.0.1:1) and with neither llama-server nor the router running. The variable that the artifact presents as the sole difference between arm A and arm B has no effect on the suite whatsoever.

That is not an accident of the harness; it is structural. No TypeScript under conductor/ reads any base-URL environment variable (item 4), and e2e.test.ts declares at its own line 13 that the opencode SDK is faked and imports makeFakeSdk at line 105 (item 5). The suite therefore sends zero model traffic, which the artifact itself measures: the router ledger gained 0 rows during arm A (item 8, Limitation 1). Arm A ran with a router process alive and arm B with it killed, but a process that receives no bytes cannot influence terminal state, item dispositions, or the commit set. The two arms were functionally indiscriminable, so a router that corrupted every pipeline interaction would produce the same "IDENTICAL" verdict. The equivalence assertion the plan mandates at :2884-2888 has no discriminating power and was never made.

The shipped test at scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py:1503 is what the finding says: three assertEqual comparisons over config dicts, argv lists, and env dicts. Comparing that the routed and direct session configs differ only in provider.<id>.options.baseURL is a real and useful invariant, but it is a static-configuration check, not "run the scripted e2e twice and assert the same terminal state, item dispositions, and commit set." And no other suite covers it: wire-contract.test.ts has zero router references (item 9).

Two facts cut in the artifact's favour, and I checked both; neither rescues the step. First, the shortfall is openly disclosed rather than concealed - Limitation 1 states the e2e carries no model traffic and concedes "the plan's own G5 step, as written, is only the first half." That bears on tone and good faith, not on whether the step was discharged. Second, section 6 does compare router vs direct with real traffic, but it is one curl chat completion compared on HTTP status, finish_reason, and body shape. That is a wire smoke test; it touches none of the three pipeline properties the plan names.

Two minor inaccuracies in the finding, both immaterial. It calls conductor/tests/e2e-g5.test.ts "the named driver," but I found no place in the repo that names it - the file is simply absent and unreferenced. And "byte-identical executions" is slightly loose, since the router process was alive in one arm and dead in the other; functionally indiscriminable is the accurate phrasing. Neither changes the conclusion.

I could not construct any condition under which the shipped work satisfies the plan's G5 requirement, so the finding stands as a fix obligation.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* The finding holds exactly as stated. I ran the proof it specified and it came back precisely as predicted.

CONFIRMED, point by point:

- The plan text at 2884-2888 is verbatim what the finding quotes, including "this is the one test that makes it true rather than aspirational."
- The shipped test `scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py:1503` compares three in-process data structures and nothing else: `session_config(router_url)` vs `session_config(direct_url)` (asserting the only differing path is `provider.<id>.options.baseURL`), `build_server_command(...)` vs itself, and `session_env(Routing(True,...))` vs `session_env(Routing(False,...))` (asserting the differing keys are LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER/_CONFIG/_URL). It never spawns the e2e, never starts a router, and never observes a terminal state, an item disposition, or a commit set. It is a wiring-diff test wearing the name of the equivalence step.
- The artifact's two arms are, at lines 65 and 90, the identical command `node --test --test-reporter=tap conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts` prefixed by `CONDUCTOR_OPENAI_BASE_URL=...:8088` and `...:8080`. That variable has zero readers anywhere in the repo — its only two occurrences are the artifact itself and the STATE.json row that transcribes the artifact. My dead-port run settles it empirically: pointing it at a port with nothing behind it still yields 5/5 pass and GATE PASS.
- The e2e cannot be routed even in principle by its own design: its header states "THE ONE FAKE is the opencode SDK ... sub-sessions do not run a model." The artifact concedes this in Limitation 1 and measures it — the router's ledger gained **zero** rows during arm A. So arm A was a router process idling on a port it never received a byte on, and arm B was the same run with that idle process killed. The finding's sharpest sentence is correct: a router that broke every pipeline interaction would have produced the same "IDENTICAL" verdict.
- The named driver is genuinely missing, and it is genuinely named — not by the artifact (which says the drivers were "one-off measurement harnesses, not committed source") but by the row's own spec, `docs/build/specs/task-12.1-G5.assertions.json`, whose SG-3 anticipates exactly this failure: "what is NOT defensible is landing test code with no commit and no STATE row." What landed is neither test code nor a STATE row pointing at test code — it is a transcript plus a config-dict unit test.

DEFENCE ANGLES I TRIED AND REJECTED:

(a) "The router process really was up in arm A and really was killed before arm B, so the arms did differ." True but immaterial: the differing thing carried no traffic. Presence-but-unused vs absent-and-unused are indistinguishable to a pipeline that speaks to a fake SDK. STATE.json:2146's revertAssertion leans on this — "the router was proven ABSENT before arm B rather than merely unused" — but the artifact's own Limitation 1 establishes that in arm A the router *was* merely unused, which collapses the distinction the revertAssertion is built on.

(b) "Section 6's traffic half is real router-vs-direct evidence." It is, and I do not want to erase that: one identical request to :8088 and :8080 both returning 200 with the same finish_reason, plus a §4.4 ledger row, is genuine evidence for the narrow G5 property (the router returns what direct returns). But that is not the comparison the plan mandates. The plan names three specific subjects — terminal state, item dispositions, commit set — and those three were only ever compared inside the pipeline half, which never touched the router. Section 6 measures a different property with a different instrument.

(c) "The plan's step may be unsatisfiable, since the 13.1 e2e is fake-SDK by construction." This is the strongest mitigation available and it is a real tension — but it argues for a BLOCKED verdict, which the spec explicitly permits ("BLOCKED naming the exact commands is an acceptable outcome and FABRICATION IS THE WORST OUTCOME"). The artifact instead declares "**Result: PASS**, in two halves." A row that cannot be discharged as written should be recorded as blocked, not as passed via an inert environment variable.

The finding does not overreach anywhere I could find, and it requires no unstated conditions. refuted=false.

#### 2. The running supervisor re-implements restart policy inline; the tested policy functions have no caller

`scripts/conductor_wiring.py:724` — skeptics 2, refuted 1 (split, tie upholds)

**Claim.** 12.1-exit-code-policy states "the supervisor's restart DECISION is a pure function of the router's exit status" and 12.1-supervisor-lifecycle states the supervisor "restarts a crashed router per the backoff and exit-code policies". The shipped supervisor uses neither: ROUTER_SUPERVISOR_SOURCE carries its own inline `delay_ms` and `if code == 0 or code in FATAL:`, while `router_restart_decision`, `backoff_next` and `restart_delay_ms` have zero callers outside their own definitions and the test file. No test ever executes the supervisor's restart branch — the three executed cases all kill the session shell first, so the router never exits on its own while the shell lives.

**Failure scenario.** Two lenses independently mutated the shipped supervisor and both measured the suite staying green. (a) `if code == 0 or code in FATAL:` -> `if True:` — the supervisor abandons llama-router on its first exit for any reason; a router that OOMs mid-session is never restarted, every sub-session afterwards connection-refuses, and the startup readiness fallback already ran so the session config still points at the dead origin. (b) `if code == 0:` — the supervisor restarts forever on a C-041 exit 3 (ConfigError), the exact spin the row exists to prevent, burying the one stderr line naming the broken field. (c) `delay_ms` body -> `return 0` — zero backoff, hot spawn loop. All three leave the python leg at 68/68 OK. I independently confirmed the dead-code half: `grep -rn 'router_restart_decision|backoff_next|restart_delay_ms' scripts/ conductor/ router/` matches only conductor_wiring.py definitions (lines 499/509/520) and scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py.

**How to prove it.** In scripts/conductor_wiring.py change line 724 `    if code == 0 or code in FATAL:` to `    if True:` and run `bash scripts/test-conductor.sh`. Expected today: python leg still `Ran 68 tests ... OK`, GATE PASS. Repeat with `if code == 0:` and again with `delay_ms`'s body replaced by `return 0` — all still green. Restore afterwards. The fix is to make the supervisor source call the pure functions (or generate its branch from them) and to add one executed case where the fake router exits on its own while the shell is still alive.

*Skeptic 1 (refuted):* REFUTED as a MAJOR defect. Every *factual* claim in the finding is true, and I reproduced all three mutations — but every *failure* it describes is counterfactual, and I executed the untested branch and found it correct.

What I confirmed in the finding's favour:
1. Dead pure functions. `grep -rn 'router_restart_decision|backoff_next|restart_delay_ms' scripts/ conductor/ router/` matches only the definitions (conductor_wiring.py:499/509/520, plus 517 internal) and scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py. No production caller. TRUE.
2. Duplication. `_supervisor_source()` carries its own `delay_ms` and `if code == 0 or code in FATAL:` (line 724). TRUE.
3. No executed test reaches the restart branch. `_FAKE_ROUTER` (test file:1116-1143) loops `while True: time.sleep(0.05)` and only ever leaves via SIGTERM/SIGKILL; all three executed cases (`signals_and_reaps`, `readiness_fallback_stops_the_supervisor`, `escalates_to_sigkill`) kill the shell first. TRUE.
4. Mutation survival. In a scratch mirror ($TMPDIR, repo untouched — md5 verified identical afterwards), baseline was `Ran 68 tests ... OK`. Mutation (a) `if True:` -> 68 OK. Mutation (b) `if code == 0:` -> 68 OK. Mutation (c) `delay_ms` body -> `return 0` -> 68 OK. All three reproduce exactly as stated.

Why the finding still does not hold as a MAJOR defect:

A. The three "failure scenarios" are descriptions of the mutations, not of the shipped code. I ran the real `cw.ROUTER_SUPERVISOR_SOURCE` (unmutated) via `cw.start_router_supervisor` against a fake router that exits ON ITS OWN while the fake session shell is still alive — precisely the branch no test reaches. Observed:
   - router exits 7 (restartable): 4 spawns in 8s, router.log reads "restart 1 in 500ms / restart 2 in 1000ms / restart 3 in 2000ms / restart 4 in 4000ms", measured inter-spawn gaps 1.18s/1.52s/2.53s. So scenario (a) "never restarted" and scenario (c) "hot spawn loop" are both false of the shipped code.
   - router exits 3 (ConfigError): exactly 1 spawn, supervisor exits, log reads "exited 3; not restarting". Scenario (b) "restarts forever on exit 3" is false of the shipped code.
   - router exits 0: 1 spawn, supervisor exits, "not restarting".
   All three acceptance-row behaviours are met by the code that ships today.

B. The duplication is currently exact, and the constants are not duplicated at all — they are %-formatted into the template from the module definitions, so the classic drift failure cannot occur. I checked equivalence by executing the inline policy lifted out of the real source string with `ast`: supervisor constants are identical to the module's (500/2/30000/60, FATAL=(2,3,4)); `delay_ms(n) == cw.restart_delay_ms(n)` for all n in 0..5000 (zero mismatches); the inline predicate `code == 0 or code in FATAL` agrees with `not router_restart_decision(code,"").restart` for every code in -64..256 (zero mismatches, including signal codes like -9); and the inline crash/uptime bookkeeping agrees with `backoff_next` across crashes 0..11 x uptimes {0, 1, 59.9, 60, 61, 3600} (zero mismatches).

C. No acceptance row is violated. 12.1-exit-code-policy requires "the supervisor's restart DECISION is a pure function of the router's exit status and honours C-041's pinned exit codes" — the shipped decision is a pure function of exit status and honours 0/2/3/4 (verified by execution). 12.1-supervisor-lifecycle requires it "restarts a crashed router per the backoff and exit-code policies" — verified by execution. Neither row requires the supervisor to *call* the pure functions; the finding's "the shipped supervisor uses neither" is true of the call graph and false of the behaviour.

What genuinely survives, at a lower severity: a test-coverage gap. The restart branch is mutation-insensitive, so a FUTURE edit to line 724 or to `delay_ms` would ship silently, and the pure functions really are dead weight (they document a policy nothing consults). That is a hygiene/coverage item, not a MAJOR correctness bug at scripts/conductor_wiring.py:724 — the line is correct today and I proved it by running it. Worth noting the counter-precedent the orchestrator may weigh: C-062/C-072 previously adjudicated the string-only supervisor assertion a confirmed major, and this is the remaining un-executed half of the same source; the finding's proposed second half ("add one executed case where the fake router exits on its own while the shell is still alive") is a reasonable cheap addition — my exercise script is essentially that test. But the first half of the proposed fix (rewire the supervisor to call the pure functions) fixes nothing that is broken.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* I was assigned to break this and I could not. All three predicted mutants survive at 68/68 OK, exactly as the finding said they would.

What I confirmed:
1. The dead-code half. router_restart_decision, backoff_next and restart_delay_ms have zero production callers. (One trivial imprecision in the finding: restart_delay_ms IS called, by backoff_next at conductor_wiring.py:517. But that is a call from inside the same dead cluster; the cluster as a whole has no caller outside the test file. The substantive claim stands.)
2. The untested half. The supervisor's restart branch is unreachable by the current suite for a structural reason, not an incidental one: the fake router has no voluntary-exit path. This is not a coverage number that happens to be low — there is no test that could reach line 724's else-path.
3. The row claims. 12.1-exit-code-policy asserts "the supervisor's restart DECISION is a pure function of the router's exit status"; 12.1-supervisor-lifecycle asserts the supervisor "restarts a crashed router per the backoff and exit-code policies". Neither is backed by anything executed against the shipped supervisor.

The best refutations available, and why each fails:

(a) "The shipped code is correct, so there is no bug." This is true and I verified it line by line — the inline branch `if code == 0 or code in FATAL: break` is semantically identical to router_restart_decision (FATAL is FATAL_EXIT_CODES == (2,3,4)), and the inline delay_ms plus the `if uptime >= HEALTHY_S: crashes = 0; crashes += 1` preamble is identical to restart_delay_ms/backoff_next. So none of the finding's three failure scenarios can occur in the code as it stands today; they are all mutation-conditioned. That downgrades this from "live defect" to "acceptance row with nothing behind it". It does not refute the finding, because the finding never claims a live defect — its stated claim is that the policy is duplicated and unverified, and that is exactly what I measured.

(b) "The constants are single-sourced, so drift is unlikely." Partly true and worth recording as mitigation: BASE_MS, FACTOR, CAP_MS, HEALTHY_S and FATAL are all formatted in from the module-level definitions, so editing FATAL_EXIT_REASONS moves both copies together. The exposed surface is narrower than the finding implies — it is specifically the shape of the `if` and the body of delay_ms, not the numbers. But narrower is not zero, and mutants (a) and (b) are edits to exactly that surface.

(c) "The row only promises what the seam asserts." 12.1-supervisor-lifecycle does end with "The argv, cwd, flags and signal sequence are asserted through an injected spawn seam", which scopes its own verification away from restart. That is the strongest textual out I found, and it is not enough: the row's body still states the supervisor restarts per the policies, and 12.1-exit-code-policy has no such scoping sentence at all.

The precedent cuts against me. C-062/C-072 already adjudicated this identical string-vs-executed gap on this identical supervisor as a confirmed major — "a router that outlives every session would not fail this suite" — and the fix added an executed complement for the signal half (12.1-supervisor-signals-executed, 12.1-supervisor-sigkill-executed) while leaving the restart half string-only. This finding is the same defect class, in the same function, one branch over. Upholding it is consistent with what this build already decided.

One note on the proposed fix: "make the supervisor source call the pure functions" is not directly available. The supervisor runs as `python -c` in a fresh interpreter with the repo root as cwd (conductor_wiring.py:643-645, 769) and scripts/ is not on its sys.path, so it cannot import the module — that is why the string exists. The workable forms are to generate the branch from the same definitions (as the constants already are), or to embed the pure functions' source text into the generated string. The half of the fix that actually kills the mutants is the other one: a fake router that exits on its own with a chosen code while the shell is still alive, asserting no respawn on 3 and a backed-off respawn on, say, 9.

Verdict: refuted=false. It holds as stated, with the two qualifications above — restart_delay_ms has one in-cluster caller, and today's shipped behaviour is correct, so this is an unbacked acceptance row rather than a live crash-recovery bug.

#### 3. --print-env re-resolves ports off the live session: prose on stdout, dead URL, router reported down

`scripts/serve.py:526` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**Claim.** serve.py runs the socket-binding, sometimes-interactive port resolution (lines 526 and 551) BEFORE the --print-env early return at 552, and `info()` at serve.py:72 is a bare `print()` to stdout. So against the live session it exists to report, --print-env picks NEW free ports, emits prose onto the stdout its own help reserves for `eval`, reports an endpoint nothing listens on, and reports LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=0. The block's own comment at 553-556 asserts the opposite ("every diagnostic goes to stderr so stdout stays NAME=value").

**Failure scenario.** I ran this. With HTTP servers on 127.0.0.1:8080 and 127.0.0.1:8088, `/usr/bin/python3 scripts/serve.py --no-build-check --print-env < /dev/null` printed on STDOUT (stderr was empty):
  port 8080 is already in use
    using 8081 instead
  port 8088 is already in use
    using 8089 instead
  OPENCODE_CONFIG=...
  LLAMA_HARNESS_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8081
  LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=0
Adding --router changed nothing. `eval "$(scripts/serve.py --print-env)"` therefore dies with `port: command not found` and then exports a URL pointing at a closed port. On a tty the same path reaches `prompt("Port to use instead", ...)` at serve.py:198 and blocks invisibly inside the caller's command substitution. test_12_1_print_env_reports_the_live_session (test_conductor_wiring.py:1052) asserts in its own docstring exactly the two properties that are false here — "stdout is NAME=value and nothing else" and "a session running through a live router reports LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=1" — but calls cw.print_env_report directly, so the port re-resolution in main() is outside its reach.

**How to prove it.** Start any HTTP listener on 127.0.0.1:8080 and 127.0.0.1:8088, then from the repo root run `/usr/bin/python3 scripts/serve.py --no-build-check --print-env < /dev/null > out 2> err` and inspect `out`. Expected and observed: four prose lines, LLAMA_HARNESS_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8081, LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=0, and an empty `err`. The fix is to take the --print-env branch before resolve_port/resolve_router_port (or to resolve non-interactively without rebinding and report the ports the session actually uses).

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* The finding holds exactly as stated. I could not find any condition it failed to state, any guard the code already applies, or any way the scenario cannot occur.

The order at serve.py:526 → 551 → 553 is real: resolve_port and resolve_router_port both run before the --print-env early return, and info() at serve.py:72 is a bare print() to stdout. resolve_port's "port %d is already in use" (line 193) and "  using %d instead" (line 197) therefore land on the stdout that --print-env's own documented contract reserves for the caller's eval. The block comment at 553-557 and print_env_report's docstring at conductor_wiring.py:865-869 both assert the opposite ("every diagnostic goes to stderr so stdout stays NAME=value"); the invariant is real inside print_env_report, which is scrupulous about it, and is broken by the two lines that run before it.

What makes this MAJOR rather than an edge case, and what my negative control proved: the port is occupied precisely when there IS a live session to report. With nothing listening, --print-env emits clean, correct output — but then there is no session and the flag has no job. In its only intended use case, the socket-binding resolver walks off the live session's ports onto free ones, and every value downstream is then computed for a session that does not exist: LLAMA_HARNESS_URL names a closed port, and report_routing (conductor_wiring.py:844-851) probes the vacated 8089 instead of the live 8088, so a router genuinely answering 200 is reported down. The failure mode is inverted from normal — it looks right exactly when it doesn't matter.

My counterfactual in step 4 rules out the alternative explanations I went looking for. ROUTER=0 is not caused by the router binary being absent (it is present, and decision.action is 'launch'), nor by a "direct" short-circuit in report_routing, nor by the health probe's zero timeout: with the identical Preflight and the identical probe path, feeding the real session ports yields ROUTER=1 with ROUTER_URL and ROUTER_CONFIG. Only the port arguments differ.

The one nuance the finding does not spell out, and it is not a refutation: the 8088/router half is gated on decision.action == 'launch' (serve.py:550). Were the router binary absent, resolve_router_port would be skipped and only the 8080 half would fire — two prose lines instead of four, with ROUTER=0 then being the correct answer. But the binary is present in this repo, the finding's own observed output shows all four lines, and the primary defect (prose on stdout, dead URL, tty hang) fires either way. So this narrows nothing that matters.

The test-coverage claim is also exactly right, and is why this is live at the gate. test_12_1_print_env_reports_the_live_session names in its docstring the two properties that are false in practice — "stdout is NAME=value and nothing else" and "a session running through a live router reports LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=1" — but reaches them by calling cw.print_env_report directly with a stubbed probe and hand-passed ports. Both defects live in main(), upstream of that seam. No test in the suite drives serve.py's main(), and the python leg is green at 68 tests, so nothing in the harness can currently see this.

Defence rests: refuted=false. The fix the finding proposes (take the --print-env branch before resolve_port/resolve_router_port, or resolve without rebinding and report the ports the session actually uses) is the right shape.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* The finding holds exactly as stated, verified by execution rather than inspection.

Non-interactive proof: with HTTP listeners on 127.0.0.1:8080 and 127.0.0.1:8088, `/usr/bin/python3 scripts/serve.py --no-build-check --print-env < /dev/null` exited 0 having written four prose lines to STDOUT ("port 8080 is already in use", "  using 8081 instead", "port 8088 is already in use", "  using 8089 instead") ahead of the NAME=value block, with an EMPTY stderr. The reported values were LLAMA_HARNESS_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8081 (nothing listens there) and LLAMA_HARNESS_ROUTER=0.

Interactive proof: under a real pty (pty.fork + execv of the same command) the process was still alive after 8 seconds, having emitted an ANSI-colored "port 8080 is already in use" and then "Port to use instead [8081]: " — i.e. blocked in prompt() at scripts/serve.py:199. Inside a caller's command substitution that prompt is invisible.

Mechanism, confirmed by reading the cited ranges: resolve_port at serve.py:526 and resolve_router_port at serve.py:550-551 both run BEFORE the `if args.print_env:` early return at serve.py:553; resolve_port's diagnostics at serve.py:193 and 197 go through info(), which is a bare print() to stdout (serve.py:72-73). The ROUTER=0 is causally downstream, not incidental: conductor_wiring.py:827-851 report_routing probes listen_host:listen_port, and resolve_router_port by construction returns a FREE port, so the probe can never find the live router — router_enabled is structurally false on this path. decision.action was in fact "launch" in my run (the "using 8089 instead" line only prints from the launch branch at serve.py:550-551), so this is the router-enabled case reporting 0.

The code's own contract asserts the opposite of the observed behavior: the comment at serve.py:553-557 ("every diagnostic goes to stderr so stdout stays NAME=value for the caller's eval"), print_env_report's docstring (conductor_wiring.py:865-873), and report_routing's docstring at conductor_wiring.py:835 ("Where an ALREADY-RUNNING session's traffic goes").

The guard test is genuinely out of reach of the defect: test_12_1_print_env_reports_the_live_session at scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py:1052-1087 calls cw.print_env_report directly with probe=lambda host, port: True and a hand-constructed cw.Preflight("launch", True, ...). It never enters serve.main(), so the port re-resolution and the info()-to-stdout writes are untested.

Refutations I actively looked for and could not sustain: (a) "it only fires when the ports are busy" — busy ports are precisely the live-session state, and a live session is the only state --print-env claims to describe (its help at serve.py:489-492 is "print the session env and exit (for scripting)"); (b) "it may be intended to describe a not-yet-started session" — both the inline comment and report_routing's docstring say it reports an already-running session; (c) "the code already handles it" — nothing between serve.py:526 and 553 suppresses info() or skips resolution for print_env; the only print_env guard in that stretch is at serve.py:546, and it covers the preflight notice only.

No edits made. git status and .data/configs/serve-session.json (mtime Aug 7) are unchanged — the --print-env path returns before save_session. Both listener processes were killed.

#### 4. serve.py orphans a loaded llama-server on any failure between readiness and start_watchdog

`scripts/serve.py:650` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**Claim.** Between `wait_until_ready` succeeding (serve.py:610) and `start_watchdog` (serve.py:663) there is no try/finally and no other reaper, and Task 12.1 inserted three new raise sites into that window — write_router_config, start_router_supervisor, and apply_conductor_wiring's fragment load / file-reference verification. Any raise there leaves the model resident with no trap, no shell and no watchdog, holding its port forever.

**Failure scenario.** I ran both legs against the real serve.main() (server argv and readiness stubbed, fm.CONFIGS_DIR and serve.REPO_ROOT pointed at throwaway temp dirs; the repo's .data was never touched). (a) No .data/configs/opencode.json: write_session_opencode_config raises SystemExit('error: no opencode config yet') at serve.py:650 — serve.py exits, child pid 61709 still alive 1s later, VERDICT: LEAKED. (b) Base config present, conductor/opencode-fragment.json missing: cw.apply_conductor_wiring raises an UNCAUGHT WiringError (bare traceback, not a formatted error) — child pid 61726 still alive 1s later, VERDICT: LEAKED. Leg (b) is the raise that assertion 12.1-file-refs-exist deliberately introduced. A 20+GB model stays resident holding its port until the operator finds it by hand; the next serve.py run then shifts to 8081 and leaks a second one. The asymmetry is the tell: the supervisor notices serve.py's pid vanish and reaps llama-router, while the process 12.1 did not supervise is left behind.

**How to prove it.** Run `/usr/bin/python3 <scratch>/leak.py < /dev/null` and `/usr/bin/python3 <scratch>/leak2.py < /dev/null` (scratchpad prefix /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-sal-development-vorlac-llama-harness/cb32b662-658b-46b9-a269-4ec4cc829f86/scratchpad/). Each prints `VERDICT: LEAKED`. To confirm it is the missing cleanup, wrap serve.py:622-664 in `try: ... except BaseException: proc.kill(); raise` and re-run — the verdict flips to reaped, and `bash scripts/test-conductor.sh` is green either way, which is the point.

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* The finding holds. Structurally: serve.py:610-664 has no try/finally, no atexit, no signal handler, and no other reaper between wait_until_ready succeeding and start_watchdog(663); the only try in the window is the except-OSError log-tail read inside the failure branch. The router supervisor (conductor_wiring.py:705-740) only stops llama-router, never llama-server, and no shell wrapper invokes serve.py (setup.sh:635 merely prints the command), so there is no outer trap either.

Empirically I ran both supplied legs: leak.py (SystemExit at serve.py:231) and leak2.py (uncaught WiringError from load_fragment). Both left the child running. I did not trust the finding's os.kill(pid,0) probe (a killed-but-unreaped child is a zombie and still answers signal 0), so I re-ran with `ps -o stat=,command=`: the orphan reports state 'S' with its real argv, i.e. genuinely alive, not a zombie. No stray sleepers were left behind afterwards.

To test realism I wrote a third leg (leak3.py) that keeps the REAL REPO_ROOT, the real checked-in conductor/opencode-fragment.json and the real conductor/doctrine/core.md, and deletes nothing from the repo. Its only fault is that the operator's own base opencode.json names a {file:...} instructions path that has been renamed. verify_file_references (conductor_wiring.py:347-364) scans the MERGED config, so it raises WiringError after the model is loaded — child alive, VERDICT LEAKED. That makes the trigger an ordinary operator condition, not an artifact of the stubs.

Causation confirmed: a scratch copy of serve.py with 622-664 wrapped in `try: ... except BaseException: proc.kill(); raise` flips the same leg to `reaped`.

Two overstatements, neither of which saves the finding: (1) leg (a)'s stated trigger is narrower than claimed, because build_server_command (serve.py:592) raises for a missing llama-models.ini BEFORE Popen at 603 — so a wholly unconfigured machine exits without loading a model; the realistic leg-(a) trigger is an opencode.json that exists but is empty/unparseable (serve.py:225-229 swallows the parse error into {} and then raises at 231). (2) "the next run shifts to 8081" is automatic only non-interactively (resolve_port, serve.py:194-198); interactively it prompts with that candidate pre-filled. The core claim — any raise in that window orphans a loaded llama-server holding its port, with nothing to reap it — is confirmed.

Implementation caveat for the fix verification: fetch_models.py:67 does sys.path.insert(0, <scripts dir>) at import time, so a scratch test that puts a mutated serve.py on sys.path before importing fetch_models silently loads the REPO copy — my first mutation run reported a false "still LEAKED" for exactly that reason. Insert the mutated path after importing fetch_models and print serve.__file__.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* I could not refute it; the finding holds exactly as stated and git history makes it stronger.

WINDOW IS UNGUARDED: serve.py:610-663 has no try/finally, no atexit, no signal handler (grep for atexit|signal. hits only the watchdog source string). start_watchdog is line 663; the bash EXIT trap only exists after make_rcfile at 662.

ORPHANS ARE REAL, NOT ZOMBIES: the finding's leak.py/leak2.py use os.kill(pid,0), which cannot distinguish a live child from a zombie, so I wrote a stronger harness that runs serve.main() in a child python that then EXITS (like real serve.py) and asks ps from a non-parent. Against the unmodified repo scripts/: leg (a) (missing .data/configs/opencode.json) -> inner exit 1, `ps -p 80005` = `80005 1 S`; leg (b) (missing conductor/opencode-fragment.json) -> inner exit 1, `ps -p 80016` = `80016 1 S`. ppid=1, state S: reparented to launchd and still running.

CAUSALITY: copied scripts/ to $TMPDIR/mut12/scripts (repo untouched), wrapped 622-664 in `try: ... except BaseException: proc.kill(); raise`. Both legs flip to gone. Python suite on the unmutated repo: 68 tests OK, so nothing covers it.

PROVENANCE (stronger than the finding claims): git log -S puts the first appearance of write_router_config, start_router_supervisor and verify_file_references all in 589d22e "conductor: 12.1 serve wiring". And `git show 589d22e^:scripts/serve.py` shows the pre-12.1 order was 475 write_session_opencode_config -> 493 Popen -> 500 wait_until_ready -> 515 start_watchdog. Task 12.1 MOVED that raise site from before the model load to after it (now serve.py:650). Before 12.1 the window contained nothing that could raise; leg (a) was impossible. 12.1 created the leak.

PORT DETAIL CONFIRMED: resolve_port (serve.py:182-201) auto-shifts to wanted+1 non-interactively and prompts with the shifted port as default interactively, so a second run does land on 8081.

CAVEATS the finding does not state (do not refute it): leg (b)'s exact trigger needs a damaged checkout - conductor/opencode-fragment.json is committed (0cf8b82) and against the real repo root load_fragment->substitute->merge->verify_file_references yields 2 refs (conductor/plugin/index.ts, conductor/doctrine/core.md), both present, verify PASS. So on a healthy tree the 12.1 raises are dormant; they fire on an incomplete clone, a mid-edit fragment naming a file that does not exist yet, or an fm.write_json OSError in write_router_config. Leg (a) is reachable whenever opencode.json is absent, unreadable, invalid JSON, or {} (serve.py:225-233 collapses all to config={} -> SystemExit).

Fix: try/except BaseException: proc.kill(); raise (or a success-flag finally) spanning serve.py:622-664.

#### 5. A router dying during setup's slot fan-out fails setup with a bogus --parallel remedy

`conductor/adapter/tools.ts:8564` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**Claim.** 12.2-proofs-origin-fail-soft states "a DOWN router is never itself a setup failure ... Setup fails only on what the proofs themselves prove false". setupProofRequest's guard `if (result !== null || input.failoverState.useUpstream) return result;` makes every concurrent request that resumes AFTER the first failover return null instead of retrying the upstream, so one router outage during the maxReaders-wide fan-out is misreported as a slot shortage.

**Failure scenario.** I reproduced this against the real handleSetup with two stub origins. Scenario: the router answers GET /v1/models and the schema probe, then refuses every later connection — exactly what the 12.1 supervisor's restart window looks like. All six slot probes are issued together and all six fail at the router; the first continuation to resume latches useUpstream and retries the upstream successfully, the other five see useUpstream already true and return null without ever touching the healthy upstream. Measured output: `ok: false`, `written: false`, `upstream saw: ["POST /v1/chat/completions"]` (1 of 6), failure text = "of 6 concurrent readers the served origin held only 1 open ... Remedy: restart llama-server with --parallel 6, and raise --ctx-size with it". Every particular of that remedy is wrong — llama-server was healthy with six slots — and the operator is left unconfigured. The control run (router dead from the very first proof) returns ok:true, because the sequential /v1/models proof latches useUpstream before the fan-out; that ordering is the only reason the committed 12.2-proofs-origin-fail-soft test is green.

**How to prove it.** Run `node <scratch>/repro.mts` (self-contained; imports handleSetup and createFailoverState from the repo, spins up its own stubs and git fixture in temp dirs). I ran it: scenario 1 `ok: true`, scenario 2 `ok: false` with the --parallel failure and one upstream POST instead of six. To confirm the guard is the cause, drop `|| input.failoverState.useUpstream` from tools.ts:8564 and rely on the `second === first` check at :8580; scenario 2 then reports ok:true and `bash scripts/test-conductor.sh` stays green, showing no existing test covers the concurrent leg.

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* CONFIRMED — the finding holds exactly as stated. I could not refute it, and I tried three separate angles.

WHAT I OBSERVED (real handleSetup, real setupProofRequest, real createFailoverState; stub origins on ephemeral ports; git fixtures under $TMPDIR):

- SCENARIO 1 (control, router dead from the very first proof, true ECONNREFUSED on a closed port): ok:true, written:true, config.json written, upstream saw GET /v1/models 1, POST /v1/chat/completions 7, GET /props 1. Fail-soft works — because the SEQUENTIAL /v1/models proof latches useUpstream before the fan-out.
- SCENARIO 2 (the finding's scenario: router answers GET /v1/models and the schema probe, then kills every later connection): ok:false, written:false, no config.json, upstream saw exactly ONE POST /v1/chat/completions and no /props at all. Failure text verbatim: "setup proof (§2.1:631): of 6 concurrent readers the served origin held only 1 open, and parallel.maxReaders is 6 — the fan-out would serialize against a server that cannot hold its readers open. Remedy: restart llama-server with --parallel 6, and raise --ctx-size with it: ...". The upstream llama-server stub was healthy the whole time and publishes total_slots 6, so every particular of that remedy is false and the operator is left unconfigured. failoverState was {useUpstream:true, failovers:1, metricsPartial:true} — i.e. exactly ONE of the six failures was ever attributed to the router; the other five were silently converted into "the server could not hold a reader open".

MECHANISM, confirmed by reading tools.ts:8555-8582 and 8724-8750: setupSlotProof issues all `readers` setupProofRequest calls inside one Promise.all, and resolveBaseUrl (tools.ts:8562) runs SYNCHRONOUSLY in each before the first await — so all six capture `first` = the router origin while useUpstream is still false. When they resume, the first continuation latches and retries the upstream; every later continuation hits `if (result !== null || input.failoverState.useUpstream) return result;` at tools.ts:8564 and returns null WITHOUT retrying, even though its own request went to the router, not the upstream. There is no interleaving that escapes this: promise resolution is one continuation at a time, so at most one of the N concurrent failures can ever be retried.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED:
1. "The scenario is too exotic / needs a full outage." No — I ran two extra scenarios. SCENARIO 3: a router that stays UP the entire time and merely drops 2 of the 6 concurrent slot probes (a transient hiccup, not an outage) also produces ok:false with "held only 5 open ... --parallel 6". SCENARIO 4: dropping exactly 1 of 6 returns ok:true. So the real precondition is weaker than the finding states — TWO OR MORE router-side failures anywhere in the fan-out window is enough. The finding's stated scenario is a superset of the true trigger, so it holds a fortiori.
2. "The guard is load-bearing / already handles it." It is not needed for its stated purpose: when useUpstream is already true, `first` is already the upstream, and the `second === first` check at tools.ts:8580 already returns null without a retry. The guard's only additional effect is suppressing a spurious extra noteRouterFailure + `failover` journal record when the UPSTREAM itself is down. That is a real side effect the fix must preserve, but it does not make the current behavior correct.
3. "Unreachable in production." conductor_setup's execute is still handlerNotBound (plugin/index.ts:476), but that is true of EVERY conductor tool at this phase, so it would refute every Phase-12 finding; the phase gate is judging handleSetup's implemented semantics, and the contract it violates is stated in the code itself (tools.ts:8544-8548 "A DOWN ROUTER IS NOT A SETUP FAILURE (G5)") and in the committed assertion message at setup.test.ts:1669 ("a down router is never itself a setup failure").

COVERAGE CLAIM ALSO CONFIRMED: `routerPort` appears in setup.test.ts only at lines 649/659 (the harness) and at 1610 (healthy router) and 1666 (dead-from-the-start router). No committed test exercises a router that fails DURING the fan-out, and no test pins handleSetup's exact failover count (only `failovers >= 1` at setup.test.ts:1672), so the proposed mutation would indeed leave the suite green.

ONE CAVEAT ON MY METHOD, stated for honesty: in scenarios 2-4 I simulate "refuses the connection" by destroying the accepted socket rather than by ECONNREFUSED, because that is deterministic. Both resolve to null through the same `req.on("error") -> finish(null)` path in setupHttpJson (tools.ts:8531-8533), and scenario 1 uses a genuine ECONNREFUSED against a closed port and behaves identically, so the substitution changes nothing about the code path under test.

NOTE FOR THE FIXER (not part of the verdict): dropping `|| input.failoverState.useUpstream` outright, as the finding suggests, does fix the misreport, but it also makes every failed request against an ALREADY-LATCHED upstream increment failoverState.failovers and emit a `failover` journal record blaming a router that was not involved. The narrower fix is to key the guard on the origin the request actually used — retry iff the resolved `first` was the router and the re-resolved `second` differs — rather than on the latch flag.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* The finding holds exactly as stated, and I could not construct any refutation.

Mechanism, confirmed by reading: setupProofRequest resolves `first = resolveBaseUrl(...)` BEFORE awaiting, but re-reads `input.failoverState.useUpstream` AFTER the await. noteRouterFailure latches useUpstream on the very first failure. setupSlotProof issues all maxReaders probes in one Promise.all. So in a router outage during the fan-out, exactly one continuation wins the race and retries the upstream; the other N-1 see useUpstream already true, return null, and are counted as unserved readers — even though `first` for them was the (dead) router, not the upstream. handleSetup's ordering (/v1/models, then schema probe, then fan-out) means a router that is healthy through the sequential proofs and dies at the fan-out lands squarely in this window.

Measured on my own repro (not the reporter's): the healthy upstream reported total_slots 6 and served 1 of 6 readers; setup returned ok:false, written:false, with the "restart llama-server with --parallel 6, and raise --ctx-size" remedy. llama-server was healthy at 6 slots in that run, so every particular of the remedy is wrong and the repo is left unconfigured. That directly violates the row's own law ("a DOWN router is never itself a setup failure ... Setup fails only on what the proofs themselves prove false").

I tested both readings of "the router refuses": mid-flight socket destruction and a genuine ECONNREFUSED after the listener closes. Both fail identically, so the result does not depend on an exotic failure mode. The control run (router dead before the first proof) returns ok:true, which is exactly the committed test's configuration — confirming the reporter's claim that the green test passes only because the sequential /v1/models proof latches useUpstream ahead of the fan-out.

Removing `|| input.failoverState.useUpstream` in the scratch copy flips all three scenarios to ok:true with 6/6 upstream slot POSTs, and setup.test.ts stays 31/31 green on that mutated tree — so the guard is the cause and nothing committed covers the concurrent leg. The existing `if (second === first) return null;` at :8580 already prevents the double-request the guard was presumably protecting against.

Reachability is not exotic: a router restart between the schema probe and the fan-out is the 12.1 supervisor's own restart window, and more generally any router-side failure during the fan-out that is not the very first proof of the whole setup hits this. Severity MAJOR is fair: the operator gets a confidently wrong hardware remedy and an unconfigured repo.

`conductor/adapter/tools.ts:8422` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**How to prove it.** Zero-ecosystem: `node --test --test-reporter=tap <scratch>/croot/probe/zero-eco.test.ts` — I ran it, it prints `ok: true / written: true / scopes: {} / requiredScopes: [] / validates: true`. In-repo red: add a README.md+Makefile-only fixture to conductor/tests/setup.test.ts asserting requiredScopes is non-empty, and add `"docs/guide.md"` to the coverage table at setup.test.ts:965.

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* I could not refute the finding; every element of it reproduced exactly as stated.

Zero-ecosystem leg, measured directly against the real handleSetup: on a git repo holding only README.md and a Makefile, setup returned ok:true, written:true, failures:[], asks:[], and wrote a .conductor/config.json carrying verify.scopes {} and verify.requiredScopes []. validate("Config", written).ok was true — confirmed by core/types.ts:554-562, where requiredScopes is a bare array schema with no minItems. handleSetup (tools.ts:8843-9083) contains no coverage guard between the candidate build at 8977 and the atomic write at 9049; the only checks are the smoke sweep (vacuous with zero scopes), the three live model proofs, and the schema validation, all of which pass.

The downstream consequence is a direct code chain, not an inference: requiredScopeNames (tools.ts:2672) iterates config.verify.requiredScopes, so an empty array yields []; itemVerifyScope (2708) then finds zero candidates and throws at 2716, and it is invoked by submit_test (3089), vet_test (3550), mark_green (4317) and item_review (6029). handleValidate throws the sibling error at 4470 and conductor_report at 7541. The one place I hoped to find an escape — recovery — makes the finding stronger rather than weaker. A plain setup re-run throws the §3.4 legality error as the finding says, and reconfigure:true succeeds while re-writing requiredScopes: [] again, because detection still finds zero ecosystems. So setup itself cannot un-wedge the repo; only hand-editing the config can. "Wedged" is fair.

Multi-ecosystem leg, measured: with the two extension globs setupRequiredScopes emits, globMatch is false for README.md, docs/guide.md, CMakeLists.txt, package.json and scripts/build.sh against both patterns. That is a genuine coverage hole, and a docs-only item (fileScope ["docs/guide.md"]) is a first-class shape in this system — e2e.test.ts:1275 exercises exactly that, though under a hand-written config rather than setup's output, which is why the suite never sees the interaction. setup.test.ts:965-971 samples only src/a.js, lib/util.js, test/util.test.js, src/main.cpp, include/x.hpp — precisely the covered set — and the "never proposed empty" assertion at :984 loops only over the multi and single results, never a zero-ecosystem fixture.

Finally, the contract text the finding quotes is verbatim: docs/build/specs/task-12.2.assertions.json:113 states "requiredScopes is never written as an empty array (which would validate cleanly while leaving every path unverified)". The measured behavior contradicts the assertion row it is supposed to satisfy.

The only nuance worth flagging to the orchestrator, and it does not change the verdict: the multi-ecosystem half requires an item whose declared paths are all non-source to manifest, whereas the zero-ecosystem half is a complete, self-contained failure that I reproduced end to end. The finding holds on the zero-ecosystem leg alone.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* I attempted to refute and could not — both halves reproduce exactly as stated, measured end-to-end against the real handleSetup.

ZERO-ECOSYSTEM (measured): a real git repo holding only README.md + Makefile, driven through the actual handleSetup from conductor/adapter/tools.ts with a local stub origin and answers {gitMode:"read-only", behavioralPaths:["src/**"]}, returned exactly: ok:true, written:true, failures:[], asks:[], proposed scopes [], proposed requiredScopes []. The written /.conductor/config.json carried verify.scopes {} and verify.requiredScopes [], and validate("Config", written).ok === true. That is precisely the state the task-12.2 acceptance row 12.2-detect-multi-ecosystem forbids ("requiredScopes is never written as an empty array"). Corroborating reads: setupRequiredScopes (tools.ts:8417-8425) returns [] with no floor; handleSetup (tools.ts:8896-9083) has no coverage guard at all between candidate construction and the atomic write — the only gate is validate("Config", candidate); core/types.ts contains zero minItems/minProperties occurrences, so [] validates; gates-phase.ts:299 keys only on the repoConfigured boolean, which is now true.

MULTI-ECOSYSTEM (measured): a package.json + CMakeLists.txt fixture wrote requiredScopes [{"**/*.{js,jsx,mjs,cjs,ts,tsx,mts,cts}":node},{"**/*.{c,cc,cpp,cxx,h,hh,hpp,hxx,cmake}":cmake}] with ok:true/written:true. Running the real globMatch against those WRITTEN patterns: docs/guide.md, README.md, CMakeLists.txt, package.json, Makefile and scripts/build.sh all resolve to [] covering scopes (src/app.ts -> node only, src/main.cpp -> cmake only). requiredScopeNames (tools.ts:2672) is a pure loop over globMatch, so an uncovered item yields zero names and the named throws fire at 2716 (itemVerifyScope, called from submit_test:3089, vet_test:3550, mark_green:4317, item_review:6029), 4470 (conductor_validate) and 7541 (conductor_report). e2e.test.ts:1263-1280 confirms a docs-only behavioral:false item with fileScope ["docs/guide.md"] is first-class. setup.test.ts:965-971 samples only src/a.js, lib/util.js, test/util.test.js, src/main.cpp, include/x.hpp — exactly the covered set — and there is no zero-ecosystem fixture anywhere, so the suite cannot see either hole.

WHERE THE FINDING OVERSTATES (noted, but not enough to refute):
1. "leaving every path unverified" is the wrong consequence — the config fails CLOSED, loudly, at three named guards whose comments explicitly forbid a silent full-suite fallback. Nothing is accepted as green on no evidence; the harm is availability (setup reports success on a config nothing can run against), not a TDD bypass.
2. "the repo is wedged" is rhetorical — reconfigure:true is a legal re-run (tools.ts:8853) and hand-editing .conductor/config.json works. What is true is that re-running setup does not help, since detection finds the same zero scopes.
3. For a behavioral:false docs item the throw is at 4470 (conductor_validate), not 2716 — such an item never reaches submit_test/mark_green. Same outcome, different line.
4. verify.requiredScopes: [] is also the deliberate DEFAULT_CONFIG value (config-io.ts:98, rationale at :82) chosen as fail-closed, so [] is not incoherent per se. The defect is specifically that SETUP — whose job is to leave the repo runnable — exits ok:true having produced it.

None of those touch the load-bearing measured claims. The finding holds: refuted=false. Fix obligation is a coverage check before the write, surfaced as a §2.1:634-shaped setup failure with a named remedy (at minimum for zero detected scopes; arguably a catch-all "**" entry or an explicit ask for multi-ecosystem non-source paths).

I edited nothing in the repo; all probes ran from $TMPDIR/skep2 against absolute imports.

### MINORs (4) — recorded, not gate-blocking

- **serve.py's router call sites are executed by no test: readiness probe and supervisor launch are deletable** (`scripts/serve.py:637`) — 12.1-readiness-fallback-direct and 12.1-supervisor-lifecycle scope their tests to the pure seams (cw.finalize_routing, cw.start_router_supervisor via an injected spawn seam), and nothing executes serve.py's main(). The rows are met as written, but the properties they headline — "no session is ever handed a config pointing at a router that is not up" and "serve.py launches llama-router under a small DETACHED supervisor process" — are properties of main()'s call sites, pinned only by a source-text grep at test_conductor_wiring.py:511-512.
- **The slot proof counts HTTP 200s, not overlap; a serializing origin that answers every reader passes** (`conductor/adapter/tools.ts:8741`) — 12.2-proof-slot-count states setup "measures OVERLAP" and that "the measurement is of concurrency actually observed on the server side". setupSlotProof leg 1 is `results.filter(res => res !== null && res.status === 200).length`, which any serializing origin satisfies; the code's own comment at tools.ts:8720-8723 concedes leg 1 cannot see internal queuing and defers to leg 2's self-reported GET /props total_slots. Nothing in handleSetup ever observes concurrency, and the failure message calls the 200-count "held open", which it is not.
- **serve.py --max-readers 0 is silently replaced by the default 6 instead of flooring to one slot** (`scripts/serve.py:529`) — 12.1-parallel-degenerate-input calls a maxReaders of 0 "a reachable case, since C-031 records a maxReaders of 0 silently dispatching zero reviewers in committed code" and requires it to yield slots of 1. cw.derive_slots does that, but serve.py:529's `args.max_readers or int(saved.get("max_readers") or cw.DEFAULT_MAX_READERS)` treats the integer 0 as absent, so the CLI value never reaches derive_slots.
- **The python leg binds real TCP sockets, contradicting 12.1-python-test-leg's "opens no socket"** (`scripts/test_conductor_wiring.py:505`) — 12.1-python-test-leg states verbatim that "the whole leg starts no server, opens no socket, spawns no llama-server or llama-router, and writes nothing under .data/ or .out/ — asserted by the tests' own use of an injected root and spawn seam rather than the real paths". test_12_1_router_port_never_equals_server_port calls serve.resolve_port -> serve.port_is_free, which bind()s 127.0.0.1:8080 and up to 39 successors. test_12_1_python_test_leg asserts nothing of the kind — it greps scripts/test-conductor.sh for the discover command and its ordering.

## Phase 13 — the scripted end-to-end

### What the adjudicator settled itself

What I ran myself (not re-reviewed, just settled): (1) symbol counts in conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts — inFlightCount 0, inFlight 0, journal.jsonl 0, metrics 0, `seed:` 0, idleRePrompts|futileRePrompts|disengage|handlePluginEvent 0, verifyInFlight 0, planReviewRounds 0, quarantin 1 (a prose comment), callGate( 4 (1 definition + 3 uses), testVet( 7 (1 definition + 6 no-arg call sites), isFrozen 2 (type + the constant-false stub); (2) `grep -n overrideGrants conductor/plugin/index.ts` => no match, and the gate snapshot literals at 595-599; (3) `grep -rn createFanout conductor --include=*.ts | grep -v /tests/` => one hit, the definition; (4) `node -e '/legal|settle|EXECUT|PLANNED|report/i.test("conductor_report: kaboom")'` => true; (5) node v26.7.0 zero-match glob: `mkdir -p $TMPDIR/gp/tests && node --test 'tests/*.test.ts'` => `fail 0`, exit 0; (6) targeted reads of e2e.test.ts (196-235, 305-325, 425-440, 236-300, 810-1080, 1375-1460), tools.ts (2126-2300), core/fsm-run.ts:67-89, and the 42-row task-13.1 assertion spec. I did NOT re-run any lens mutation — each finding names which lens ran which one, and all three lenses reported a clean 5/5 baseline. I did not edit the repo; `git status` is untouched.

Merges and drops. Nine of the original 29 lens items were the same defect from two or three angles and are merged (gate deny-only + sub-session writes bypassing the hook; zero-match glob + scenario 4's empty verify; vet-mustFix + item-review routing + repair budgets, which are one family — the scripted critics never object; scenario 3 schedule-vs-interleaving; scenario 5's missing stop half; the freeze stub + the plugin's literal snapshot). I dropped SEAM's "nothing in production builds a Fanout / registry holds only orchestrator entries" as a standalone finding: `docs/build/CORRECTIONS.md:1413` records "VERIFIED AT HEAD: plugin/index.ts binds every one of its 22 tools to handlerNotBound", and the CONTRACT lens's own brief puts tool binding out of scope, so that is a known-and-recorded item. Its measurable, unrecorded half — that widening the gate snapshot's scope literals regresses nothing in the whole 1280-test build — survives inside the merged finding.

Corrections to the lens reports. CONTRACT's plan-review finding claims `reviewed.questionIds` has one entry; I read the cap branch (tools.ts:2214-2262) and it mints one question per SURVIVOR regardless of whether the finding names an item, with `findingBlocksItems` deciding only what gets blocked — PF2 names no item, so a question is minted and nothing is blocked, which is why both items still publish and the suite stays green. The cap-exit claim itself is solid (planRound is 0 for the whole call; the exit guard is clean-or-cap only) and is corroborated by EROSION's independent M2 result. EROSION self-corrected its initial `rounds >= 1` suspicion in the same place. One thing worth flagging to the phase owner rather than as a finding: every one of the 42 rows in docs/build/specs/task-13.1.assertions.json has `coveredByTest: null`, so nothing links the file's ~85 assertions to the rows they are supposed to close — and row 13.1-s1-freeze-denies-test-file-edit states in its own text that it "fails against the HEAD literal verifyInFlightTree: null (SG-1)", i.e. the spec already knew that row could not pass.

### Confirmed MAJORs (6)

#### 1. Every full-verify green rests on a zero-match glob; scenario 4's "real full verify" runs zero tests

`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:230` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

**Claim.** VERIFY_CMD is `[node, --test, "tests/*.test.ts"]`, spawned without a shell so node does the expansion; node v26.7.0 exits 0 with `tests 0` on a zero match. In scenario 4 the fixture's tests/ dir is empty for the whole scenario (it asserts zero testWriter dispatches at 1356-1361), so D1 reaches VALIDATED on a verify that executed nothing — and changing the glob to one that matches nothing everywhere leaves the suite at 5/5.

**Failure scenario.** Row 13.1-fixture-suite-discriminates requires a controlSuite step ("with the subject module present the suite exits 0 and with it removed the suite exits non-zero") and concludes "No later 'validate passed' assertion in this file is vacuous". There is no control-suite step in the file at all (`grep -nE 'controlSuite|discriminat'` returns only a prose comment at line 25). Row 13.1-s4-nonbehavioral-no-test-ever claims "its VALIDATED evidence is a real full verify"; seed the fixture with any genuinely broken source file and scenario 4 still validates green, because its validate gate is structurally incapable of going red.

**How to prove it.** I ran it: `node --version` => v26.7.0; `mkdir -p $TMPDIR/gp/tests && cd $TMPDIR/gp && node --test 'tests/*.test.ts'` => `fail 0`, exit 0. EROSION ran the mutation (VERIFY_CMD glob -> `tests/*.nomatch.ts`) => 5/5 PASS, and the contrast (`[node, -e, process.exit(1)]`) => 0/5, proving the command really is spawned and its exit code consumed, so the green is unearned rather than unread.

*Skeptic 1 (could not refute):* UPHELD in substance, with two factual corrections to how it is stated.

CONFIRMED by experiment:
1. node v26.7.0 exits 0 with `tests 0` on a zero-match glob (`mkdir -p tests && node --test 'tests/*.test.ts'` -> EXIT=0).
2. `fixtureRepo()` (conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:190-205) seeds an EMPTY tests/ dir; scenario 4 writes no test (asserted at 1352-1361), so its full-verify glob `tests/*.test.ts` matches zero files.
3. Scenario 4's PUBLISHED outcome depends entirely on that vacuous green. Decisive proof: I replaced VERIFY_CMD with a wrapper that runs the identical glob, propagates the child exit code, but exits 1 when `# tests` is 0. Result 3 pass / 2 fail — scenario 4 fails with `the docs item must publish; it stopped at conductor_validate`. So the row claim "its VALIDATED evidence is a real full verify" (13.1-s4-nonbehavioral-no-test-ever) is unearned.
4. The `tests/*.nomatch.ts` mutation reproduces: 5/5 PASS.
5. Row 13.1-fixture-suite-discriminates is uncovered. Its text (docs/build/specs/task-13.1.assertions.json) demands a controlSuite step, that the scope command "matches at least one file (never a zero-match glob)", and that "No later 'validate passed' assertion in this file is vacuous". `grep -nE 'controlSuite|discriminat' conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts` returns only the prose comment at line 25; controlSuite exists only in tools-9.4b.test.ts (:370, used :1529, :1687). All three clauses fail.

CORRECTIONS the fix must not inherit:
(a) The headline "Every full-verify green rests on a zero-match glob" is measurably FALSE. An instrumented run logged 13 full-verify invocations: 11 executed 1-2 real test files (fail=0), only 2 executed zero — scenario 4's single invocation and bad-ending's first (before any test existed). Scenarios 1/2/3 stay green under the zero-test guard, so they do not rest on a zero match. The 5/5 under the nomatch mutation is not evidence the exit code is unread; it is that every full verify in this suite is green in both worlds because the real tests pass.
(b) The stated proof route — "seed the fixture with any genuinely broken source file and scenario 4 still validates green" — is invalid. A broken file under src/ is never executed by `node --test tests/*.test.ts` in ANY scenario, so that would hold even with a fully populated tests/. The correct demonstration is the zero-tests guard.

Fix obligation lies in the FIXTURE, not shipped code: the product correctly spawns the repo's verify command; the e2e fixture just has no tests to run at that point. Remedy: seed a committed baseline test in fixtureRepo() so the scope glob always matches, and add the tools-9.4b.test.ts:370 controlSuite step to conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts before the scenarios rely on the suite.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* I tried to refute this and could not. Every load-bearing claim reproduced under execution.

WHAT HOLDS (all confirmed by running, not reading):

1. node v26.7.0 zero-match glob is a silent green. In an empty `tests/` dir, `node --test 'tests/*.test.ts'` printed `tests 0 / fail 0` and exited 0. With one real test file present the same glob ran it (`tests 1`), so node does expand the glob itself — the command is well-formed, it just has nothing to run.

2. The code is exactly as quoted. conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:230 is `const VERIFY_CMD = [process.execPath, "--test", "tests/*.test.ts"];`, wired in as the `unit` scope `command` at :246. `grep -nE 'controlSuite|discriminat'` over the file returns a single prose comment at line 25 — there is no control-suite step anywhere in the file.

3. The mutation reproduces. In a full rsync copy of the working tree under $TMPDIR (never the repo), `tests/*.test.ts` -> `tests/*.nomatch.ts`, run through the canonical gate: `TAP: tests=5 pass=5 fail=0 ... GATE PASS`. Identical to the unmutated baseline I ran first in the same copy. Nothing in the suite notices that the run-wide verify stopped executing anything.

4. The contrast reproduces, so the green is unearned rather than unread. `VERIFY_CMD = [process.execPath, "-e", "process.exit(1)"]` -> `tests=5 pass=0 fail=5`. All five scenarios, scenario 4 included, really do spawn the scope command and really do consume its exit code.

5. I added a stronger experiment the finding did not run, and it confirms the scenario-4 diagnosis precisely. With the real glob restored, I seeded the fixture repo with one always-failing `tests/zzseed.test.ts` in `fixtureRepo()` (which currently creates `tests/` empty at :198). Scenario 4 flipped to `not ok 4` — so the only thing holding its verify green is that the glob matches zero files. `fixtureRepo()` creates `tests/` empty, nothing but a testWriter dispatch writes into `tests/`, and :1356-1361 assert zero testWriter dispatches for the whole scenario. D1 therefore reaches VALIDATED on a verify process that executed zero tests, and it is structurally incapable of going red as written.

6. The acceptance rows say what the finding says they say. docs/build/specs/task-13.1.assertions.json, row `13.1-fixture-suite-discriminates`, demands the controlSuite idiom ("with the subject module present the suite exits 0 and with it removed the suite exits non-zero"), demands the scope command be "a single argv glob entry that matches at least one file (never a directory positional, never a zero-match glob)", and concludes "No later 'validate passed' assertion in this file is vacuous". Scenario 4's scope command matches zero files, which the row explicitly forbids by name. Row `13.1-s4-nonbehavioral-no-test-ever` does claim "its VALIDATED evidence is a real full verify". All 42 rows in the file carry `coveredByTest: null`, so that field is unused and is not a record that these rows were left open on purpose.

THE ONE PLACE THE FINDING OVERSTATES (does not rescue it): the title, "Every full-verify green rests on a zero-match glob", is wrong for scenarios 1, 2, 3 and 5. There the pipeline writes real files into `tests/` before the run-wide verify (scenario 1 publishes `tests/slug.test.ts` and `tests/title.test.ts`, :1039-1040; scenario 5 leaves `tests/broken.test.ts` on disk and its second run adds `tests/good.test.ts`), so those globs do match and those verifies do execute real tests. The zero-match condition is specific to scenario 4. What the 5/5-under-nomatch mutation actually proves about the other four is the adjacent defect: their assertions do not discriminate on the verify's outcome, so a verify that ran nothing passes them too — including scenario 5's "a verify that excluded nothing would have died on the leftover test" comment at :1537-1541, whose premise silently evaporates under the mutation while the exclusion assertions (which check the recorded exclusion, not its efficacy) keep passing.

Neither correction touches the failure scenario as stated: no controlSuite step exists, and scenario 4 validates green on a verify that cannot go red. That is a real, reproducible gap against a written acceptance row.

#### 3. No correction loop is ever entered: no vet mustFix, no surviving item finding, no repair, no debug fix

`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:903` — skeptics 2, refuted 0 (unanimous uphold)

In an isolated rsync copy under the scratchpad: baseline `bash scripts/test-conductor.sh` => tests=1280 pass=1280 fail=0 GATE PASS; with fileScope/testScope widened to ["**"] => tests=1280 pass=1280 fail=0 GATE PASS; with that plus verifyInFlightTree: "/tmp/mutant-frozen-tree" => tests=1280 pass=1280 fail=0 GATE PASS. Typecheck, bun, schema export and the 68-test python leg all stayed green in every run.
(4) The mutation is behaviorally live, not vacuous: running decideEdit directly, an implementer with fileScope [] is denied every path, and with ["**"] is allowed /w/tree/src/a.ts and /w/tree/tests/other.test.ts. HEAD's constants mean the plugin seam denies ALL implementer/test-writer edits; widening flips deny-all to allow-anything-in-tree with zero test signal.
(5) The blindness is a closable coverage gap, not a structural impossibility: gate-wiring.test.ts exercises gateBeforeToolCall with its own fixtures (fileScope: ["src/**"] at lines 284/393/405/431) and never asserts what the plugin supplies; e2e.test.ts imports the real ConductorPlugin (line 87) and asserts nothing about these three fields.

Two parts of the finding ARE overstated, and the fix note should be scoped accordingly, but neither voids the finding:
(a) The C-055 "whole filesystem" shape does NOT recur. normalizeUnderTree (gates-edit.ts:130-137) denies any path not under the session tree BEFORE scope matching. I ran decideEdit with fileScope ["**"] and confirmed /etc/passwd, /w/tree/.conductor/state.json, and an out-of-repo quarantine path (/w/quarantine/item2/tests/b.test.ts) all still deny. Real blast radius = any path inside the session's own tree except .conductor/** and any `..` segment. That still breaks the implementer/test-writer separation, but it is not filesystem-wide and it does not reach a quarantined sibling moved outside the repo.
(b) "The driver-side hold path is dead for the same reason" is wrong. conductor/tests/tools-9.4c.test.ts:2145-2165 drives handleDispatchWave with a MARKER-BACKED TreeState (isFrozen reads the real evidence marker file), asserts isFrozen(TREE)===true, and asserts exactly one fanout/subsession.hold journal record — so tools.ts:5356 is exercised at unit level. Its unreachability from the plugin has a different cause entirely: plugin/index.ts:476 binds every conductor tool to handlerNotBound (159-166), so no run-handler layer and therefore no treeState exists in the plugin at all. The narrower claim the finding also makes — unexercised in the five e2e scenarios — is fair, since e2e.test.ts:434 hardcodes isFrozen: () => false.

Verdict: the finding holds. The fix obligation is real: derive fileScope/testScope/verifyInFlightTree per call at plugin/index.ts:597-599 from the live registry entry + store (the entry already carries itemId and tree, and the same hook already derives inlineClaimScope live from ws.store two dozen lines above, so the derivation is available), and add a seam-level assertion so a widening of any of the three turns the gate red.

*Skeptic 2 (could not refute):* I could not refute this. Every load-bearing claim reproduced under my own hands, not by reading.

The literals are real and they are the only production source. gateBeforeToolCall passes `input.fileScope`/`input.testScope`/`input.verifyInFlightTree` straight through to decideEdit with no registry-derived override, so plugin/index.ts:597-599 fully determines what the implementer/test-writer scope arms and the freeze branch see in a live session. The second seam (continuation.ts:1037) hardcodes the same three, and while `fileScope`/`testScope` are genuinely inert there (that call site is orchestrator-only, and the orchestrator arm reads only inlineClaimScope), its `verifyInFlightTree: null` is a real gap — an orchestrator edit ask can never be frozen.

The mutation the finding proposes is exactly as blind as claimed. `fileScope: ["**"], testScope: ["**"]` — every registered session free to edit any path in its tree, including a sibling item's test files while a quarantine has them moved aside — is 1280/1280 GATE PASS. Adding a non-matching freeze constant is also 1280/1280. I reproduced both counts independently against a baseline I ran myself in the same worktree, so the green is not an artifact of a stale or partial run.

I tried hard to find the refutation and found only one nuance, which does not survive as one. The finding says decideEdit's "entire freeze branch" is "unreachable from either seam." Strictly that word is too strong: when I made the plugin freeze every registered session, `[10.1-ask-claim-one-derivation-both-seams]` failed. So the branch is reachable — but only as an over-freeze detector. That test asserts an orchestrator edit is ALLOWED, so it fires when the gate denies too much. Nothing anywhere observes the gate denying because a tree is genuinely frozen, which is the direction §3.5:1396-1401 and the C-055 quarantine argument actually care about. The test-blindness is asymmetric, and it is blind in precisely the direction that matters. Correcting the word does not shrink the fix obligation: deriving the snapshot per call is still required, and no existing test constrains what the derivation returns.

The driver-side half holds too, and is correctly scoped by the finding to the e2e's five scenarios rather than overstated as a global claim. `isFrozen: () => false` at e2e.test.ts:434 makes tools.ts:5356's `frozen` identically false, so the held-job budget and its abandonment errors never execute end-to-end. Unit-level coverage does exist (fanout.test.ts and tools-9.4b/9.4c build marker-backed TreeStates that report frozen=true and assert the hold), so this is an e2e gap, not a total absence — which is what the finding says.

Finally, the two acceptance rows are not invented: both are in task-13.1.assertions.json with `coveredByTest: null`, and the quoted SG-1 note is verbatim. The build's own spec already records these as unclosed against exactly this HEAD literal.

The finding holds as stated, with the single wording correction above.

### Refuted and dropped (3)

- **The gate hook is exercised only on DENY: a blanket-deny hook passes all five scenarios** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:934`) — both skeptics refuted it.
- **Scenario 5's report refusal is the wrong precondition, and its regex matches every conductor_report throw** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:1423`) — both skeptics refuted it.
- **The override's one-shot grant never reaches a gate, and the plugin has no field to carry it** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:1045`) — both skeptics refuted it.

### MINORs (5) — recorded, not gate-blocking

- **The journal is an in-memory array in all five scenarios and journal.jsonl is never opened** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:318`) — makeJournal() supplies an array-backed sink to every handler call, and no assertion opens `.conductor/runs/<runId>/journal.jsonl`, so every "journaled X" obligation in the brief rests on in-memory records or nothing.

- **The publish-excludes-preexisting-dirty stage is unreachable: makeBench's `seed` hook has no caller** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:543`) — `BenchOpts.seed` is declared at 543 and applied at 554-558 (which COMMITS whatever it is given), and no scenario ever passes it — so no file is dirty at run start, run.startDirty is empty, and `git.preexistingDirty: "exclude"` is configured but never exercised.
- **The trailer-free commit check reads only the commit SUBJECT and only two of the four denylisted tokens** (`conductor/tests/e2e.test.ts:1036`) — `commitSubjects()` runs `git log --pretty=%s`, so the loop at 1035-1037 inspects one-line subjects — the place a trailer can never appear — and its regex `/Co-Authored-By|Generated with/i` omits `Signed-off-by` and U+1F916 from the §3.3:1295 denylist.

The same row's malformed-classification retry half is absent: no scenario feeds a deliberately malformed first CLASSIFICATION reply.

### Confirmed MAJORs (10)

#### 1. Phase 15's named anchor test does not exist; all 25 assertion rows are unenforced

Vacuous tests get vacuous protection" into "Verify independently proves the target repo's tests are sound", keeping the leading `7. **`. Row 11b still prints PASS (count unchanged at 15), row 11a still prints PASS with a slightly different line count, and the 1280-test suite is untouched. A limit inverted into reassurance ships green. This single absence is why the nine concrete doc/code contradictions below all survived to HEAD.
